heading: Helpdesk
simulation: Simulation: the company, the people and the cases are made up. The technology is real - every command exists, and this is what its output looks like.
count: {count, plural, =0 {No tickets} one {# ticket} other {# tickets}}
select: Choose a ticket from the list.

no-network.title: No network at desk 14
no-network.symptom: Since this morning neither the internet nor the network drive works. The cable is plugged in and the light on the network socket is on.
steps: First the computer's address: it starts with 169.254. Windows gives itself an address like that when no DHCP server answers. So the cable is fine - what is missing is an address.
A fresh request to the DHCP server goes unanswered. The problem lies with the server or on the way to it, not with this PC.
The statistics on the DHCP server show all 200 addresses in the range are taken. Most belong to smartphones on the guest Wi-Fi, which shares the range and keeps each address for eight days.
no-network.solution: The guest Wi-Fi got its own address range with a four-hour lease. Addresses in the office range were free again, and ipconfig /renew at desk 14 worked at once.
no-network.lesson: An address starting with 169.254 means the computer found no one to give it an address. The search starts at DHCP, not at the cable.

intranet-dns.title: Intranet unreachable, internet works
intranet-dns.symptom: External websites load, but intranet.talweber.example says "server not found".
steps: The intranet server answers on its IP address. So the network works - the problem is name resolution.
The name lookup goes to a public DNS server. It only knows public names; internal names are known only to the company's own DNS server.
DHCP is on, but the DNS server was entered by hand - apparently during a test while working from home - and overrides the one DHCP would supply.
intranet-dns.solution: Set DNS on the network adapter back to "obtain automatically" and cleared the cache with ipconfig /flushdns. The intranet loads again.
intranet-dns.lesson: A name and an address are two separate layers. Test the IP address first, then the name, and two commands tell you which layer is broken.

printer-postscript.title: Printer prints pages of code
printer-postscript.symptom: Instead of the invoice, dozens of pages come out starting with "%!PS-Adobe-3.0", full of characters nobody can read.
steps: The configuration page printed straight from the printer's control panel comes out clean. The printer itself is fine.
The same file prints correctly from another computer. So the problem lies between this one PC and the printer: the driver.
After an update, a PostScript driver is assigned. This printer only understands PCL, so it prints the PostScript code as plain text.
printer-postscript.solution: Installed the manufacturer's PCL 6 driver and assigned it to the printer. The invoice prints; the pile of pages went to recycling.
printer-postscript.lesson: Test each link in the chain on its own - device, network, computer. Then you find the fault instead of guessing.

print-queue.title: Nobody on the ground floor can print
print-queue.symptom: Every print job stays in the queue. Restarting their own PCs changed nothing.
steps: The queue on the print server: the first job shows "Error", every other job waits behind it.
The broken job can be deleted but stays stuck on "Deleting". The print service is holding on to it.
After restarting the print service the stuck job is gone and the waiting jobs go through.
print-queue.solution: Removed the stuck job and restarted the print spooler. The warehouse list was printed again as a PDF and went through without errors.
print-queue.lesson: A queue works in order. A single stuck job blocks everything behind it - the same principle as batch processing in the computer centre of 1956.

account-lockout.title: Account locked every morning
account-lockout.symptom: The account is locked every morning even though the password is typed correctly. Ever since the password change last week.
steps: On the domain controller, event 4740 records every lockout - and the computer the bad sign-ins came from. It is not her PC but PC-LAGER-02.
PC-LAGER-02 has a network drive connected with stored credentials - still with the old password. The computer keeps retrying with it until the account locks.
Deleted the stored credentials.
account-lockout.solution: Unlocked the account, removed the stale credentials on PC-LAGER-02 and reconnected the drive. No lockout since.
account-lockout.lesson: A lockout often comes from a forgotten device retrying an old password. Event 4740 names the sender.

slow-pc.title: PC extremely slow
slow-pc.symptom: Since Monday, programs take minutes to start. Sometimes the PC does not respond at all.
steps: Measure first: the processor is barely busy, but the disk is at 100 percent the whole time. The bottleneck is the drive.
Drive C: is almost full - 1.8 GB free. Windows can neither unpack updates nor grow the page file.
The computer still has a spinning hard disk. It is healthy, but too slow for a workstation today.
slow-pc.solution: Short term: moved large video recordings from the profile to the network drive; over 100 GB are free now. For good: an SSD is on order; the ticket is waiting for the delivery.
slow-pc.lesson: Measure, then act: processor, memory, disk. The bottleneck is rarely where you expect it.

dock-display.title: Second monitor stays black
dock-display.symptom: After moving to another desk, the second monitor stays black. The first one works.
steps: The monitor's light is orange: it has power but gets no picture.
Swapped the cable for one known to work: still black. So it was not the cable.
Connected the laptop straight to the monitor without the docking station: picture. The fault is in the docking station - its firmware is much older than at the other desks.
dock-display.solution: Updated the docking station's firmware; both monitors work now. The other docks of the same model are on the list for the next update.
dock-display.lesson: Swap a part for one you know works. Every swap halves the list of suspects.

meeting-wifi.title: Wi-Fi drops in the meeting room
meeting-wifi.symptom: The connection keeps dropping during video calls, only in this room.
steps: The laptop sits on channel 3 in the 2.4 GHz band, with a middling signal.
The neighbouring networks transmit on channels 1 and 6. Channel 3 overlaps both: in the 2.4 GHz band only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap.
The access point in the room can do 5 GHz as well, but band steering is off - so the laptops stay in the crowded 2.4 GHz band.
meeting-wifi.solution: Moved the access point to channel 11 and switched on 5 GHz with band steering. The laptops now connect at 5 GHz; the ticket stays open for a week to watch the next calls.
meeting-wifi.lesson: Radio is a shared medium. Transmit between channels 1, 6 and 11 in the 2.4 GHz band and you disturb two neighbours at once.

share-access.title: Department folder not visible
share-access.symptom: The new colleague cannot see the department folder, although she was added to the group this morning.
steps: In the directory she is a member of the group Einkauf-RW. So the permission is set correctly.
Her running session does not know the group, though: the list of groups is fixed once at sign-in, and she signed in before she was added.
After signing out and back in, the group is in the list.
share-access.solution: Signed out and back in once - the folder is there. Not a permissions problem, just a question of timing.
share-access.lesson: Group memberships take effect at the next sign-in: permissions are written into an access token when you sign in, and it does not change after that.
